Examples of Kula stress — DISYLLABIC 1st: /'mana/ ‘village’ ['ma.na], /'mɪti/ ‘sit’ ['mɪ.ti], /'lula/ ‘go’ ['lu.la], /'jɐku/ ‘two’ ['jɐ.ku]; 2nd: /mda/ ‘go.up’ [mə.'da], /a'jɐk/ ‘rice’ [a.'jɐk], /a'da/ ‘fire’ [a.'da]. TRISYLLABIC 1st: /'asɐkaˌ/ ‘tree’ ['a.sə.ˌka], /'tatuku/ ‘talk about’ ['ta.tu.ˌku]; 2nd: /ta'taku/ ‘meet, find’ [ta.'ta.ku], /dis'paka/ ‘squash’ [dis.'pa.ka]; 3rd: /balu'ne/ ‘sweet potato’ [ˌba.lu.'ne]. QUADRISYLLABIC 3rd: /ada'masa/ ‘bird’ [ˌa.da.'ma.sa], /gɐka'baku/ ‘cat’ [ˌgɐ.ka.'ba.ku], /mila'piki/ ‘lightning’ [ˌmi.la.'pi.ki]] Stress apparently makes some limited phonemic contrasts, but further analysis is required to confirm this. The minimal pair in (36) appears to contrast only in terms of stress placement. (36) /'kula/ ['ku.la] ‘split in two’ /ku'la/ [ku.'la] ~ [ku.'lua] ‘foam’ [p. 67:] Stress, although potentially phonemic, bears a low functional load and as such will not normally be marked in the orthography used here. [Donohue 1996 p. 101 fn. 1:] The phonological system of Tanglapui includes the following consonants and vowels: p t k kʷ b d g gʷ m n ŋ ŋʷ v r l y s i ɨ u e o a. Stress is non-contrastive, and initial.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable (non-contrastive) and falls on the first syllable of the word.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a phoneme-inventory footnote; no domain, citation-form, or phrase-level detail given. Language name in source: Tanglapui, Lantoka dialect (= Kula, kula1280).
new_statements.identity_note: Donohue 1996 calls the language Tanglapui and states the data come from the Lantoka dialect ('the unusual voice system that is found in the Lantoka dialect of Tanglapui'). Glottolog lists Tanglapui, Lantoka and Lamtoka as alternate names of kula1280, so this is the same language-level entity; no separate dialect glottocode was seen. Williams 2017 uses the name Kula.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (classification conflict, src world-r2-2026-09-17) quotes exactly these pages of this work, and the file confirms the quote verbatim, so nothing changes on the Williams side. Against the existing statement held by the project from Donohue 1996 ('Stress is non-contrastive, and initial', Tanglapui = the same language, the desa where Williams worked) Williams's data contradict both halves: non-initial primary stress is common (a'da 'fire', a'jɐk 'rice', ta'taku, balu'ne, ada'masa) and a stress-only minimal pair is given; that disagreement is the conflict the catalog already records. No further open copy is needed: the accessible source has been read.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Williams states no placement rule. Stress (louder, higher pitch) is a word-level property whose position varies: in his Table 7 disyllables carry primary stress on the 1st or the 2nd syllable, trisyllables on the 1st, 2nd or 3rd, and the quadrisyllabic examples on the 3rd (penultimate) syllable; one minimal pair (/'kula/ 'split in two' vs /ku'la/ 'foam') differs only in stress placement. He hedges: stress 'apparently makes some limited phonemic contrasts, but further analysis is required', is 'potentially phonemic' with 'low functional load', and is not written in his orthography. Stress interacts with vowel quality/length: the /i/-/ɪ/ and /a/-/ɐ/ contrasts are robust only in stressed syllables, stressed cardinal vowels are long (~100 ms), and unstressed initial /i/ and unstressed final high vowels are often dropped.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No prose rule; p. 60 says only that <ˌ> marks secondary stress. The Table 7 transcriptions place a secondary stress two syllables away from the primary: on the final syllable of initial-stressed trisyllables (['a.sə.ˌka] 'tree', ['ta.tu.ˌku] 'talk about') and on the initial syllable when the primary is on the third syllable ([ˌba.lu.'ne] 'sweet potato', [ˌa.da.'ma.sa] 'bird', [ˌgɐ.ka.'ba.ku] 'cat', [ˌmi.la.'pi.ki] 'lightning').
new_statements.exceptions: none framed as stress exceptions; related: deletion of unstressed initial /i/ is blocked when /i-/ is the 1pl inclusive agreement prefix (ex. 35, p. 62), and the set II prefix igá- may surface as gá- 'despite the stress falling on' it (§2.2.2); the author flags the phonemic status of stress as needing further analysis
new_statements.identity_note: Williams 2016 describes Kula (ISO tpg) as spoken in Desa Tanglapui, eastern Alor (hamlets Lantoka, Samuda/Moduda, Kaipera; data mostly from Lantoka and Samuda, recordings 2010-2014). Donohue's 'Tanglapui' is the same language named after that desa.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement, already on record as the catalog's 'conflict': Donohue 1996 (Inverse in Tanglapui, p. 101 fn. 1) says 'Stress is non-contrastive, and initial', while Williams 2016 §2.2.5 (pp. 62-63), based on four years of fieldwork in the same desa (Tanglapui: Lantoka and Samuda), gives words with primary stress on non-initial syllables in every word length (a'da 'fire', a'jɐk 'rice', ta'taku 'meet', balu'ne 'sweet potato', ada'masa 'bird') and a minimal pair distinguished only by stress placement ('kula 'split in two' vs ku'la 'foam'), calling stress 'potentially phonemic' with 'low functional load' and stating no placement rule. Williams's account is the fuller and later one but is explicitly hedged ('further analysis is required'); the Internet Archive copy read here is the same file the catalog record was built from, so the re-read adds no new fact and changes no reading.
